metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Tallying heuristic (i.e., choosing the option that wins on the most features, ignoring validities). Ties are excluded. The advocated theory (Tallying) will score highly on this metric. The competing theory (WADD) will score lower because it will frequently choose an option with fewer winning features if those features have higher validities (e.g., in Trial 1, WADD often prefers Option A which has 2 high-validity features, whereas Tallying prefers Option B which has 3 low-validity features).

This metric calculates the proportion of choices consistent with the WADD model on the critical trials where WADD and Tallying make opposite predictions. Specifically, it looks at trials where one option has the top two most valid features and the other option has the bottom three. WADD prefers the option with the top two features because their combined validity outweighs the bottom three, whereas Tallying prefers the option with the bottom three features because it simply counts the number of winning features (3 vs 2). Thus, WADD will score highly on this metric, while Tallying will score poorly.

In this 6-feature experimental design, Trials 2, 4, 5, 6, and 7 all pit an option with exactly 2 positive features against an option with exactly 4 positive features. Crucially, the 2-feature option always consists of two of the top 3 highest-validity features, while the 4-feature option consists of the remaining one top-tier feature plus all three of the bottom-tier features. The Take The Best (TTB) heuristic, driven by a noisy cue hierarchy, will choose the 2-feature option whenever either of its two top-tier features happens to be ranked first (approximately 2/3 of the time). In stark contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all features; because the sum of validities for the 4-feature option (~2.6) substantially outweighs the sum for the 2-feature option (~1.7), WADD will systematically prefer the 4-feature option. Measuring the proportion of times the subject chooses the 2-feature option in these specific trials creates a powerful, low-variance discriminator: it will be high (~0.66) for TTB and very low (~0.0) for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses Option B in trials where Option B has the highest-validity feature (feature 0) and Option A lacks it, but Option A has a compensatory advantage in the number of lower-validity features (sum >= 3). The Take The Best (TTB) heuristic will almost always choose Option B because it relies solely on the first discriminating feature (feature 0). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all features, allowing Option A's multiple lower-validity features to compensate for its deficit on the highest-validity feature, leading to a much lower rate of Option B choices.

In all 8 trial pairs of this design, the highest-validity feature (the rightmost one) perfectly contradicts the leftmost discriminating feature. Take The Best (TTB) prioritizes features by validity (right-to-left in this design), leading to choices that align with the rightmost feature. Take The First (TTF) evaluates features strictly left-to-right, leading to choices that align with the leftmost feature. By calculating the proportion of trials where the subject's response aligns with the rightmost feature, TTB will score highly (close to 1.0, modulo noise), while TTF will score very lowly (close to 0.0, modulo noise). This creates an extremely stark contrast between the two models.

This metric computes the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the prediction of the Take The First (Left-to-Right) heuristic. Since the experimental design specifically pits the left-to-right reading order against the objective validities (where the highest validities are in the middle), the Take The First model will score very high on this metric. Conversely, the Take The Best model, which prioritizes the middle features, will systematically make choices opposed to the left-to-right prediction on key trials, resulting in a significantly lower score.

In all experimental trials, exactly one option possesses the most valid feature (Feature 0, validity 0.95). The Take The Best (TTB) model predicts that subjects will predominantly choose the option with this highest-validity feature, resulting in a proportion significantly greater than 0.5. In contrast, the Random Choice / Minimal Effort model predicts that choices will be heavily influenced by a near-total lapse rate, pulling the proportion of choices for the Feature 0 option very close to 0.5. Measuring the overall proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with Feature 0 = 1 will effectively discriminate between the systematic preference of TTB and the random guessing of the competing theory.

The Random Choice theory predicts that subjects will guess with probabilities very close to 0.5 on all trials, meaning the empirical proportion of choosing Option B will tightly cluster around 0.5 (subject only to binomial noise). The Take The Best (TTB) theory predicts systematic preferences on most trials driven by the highest-validity discriminating cue, pushing choice proportions towards 0 or 1. By calculating the mean absolute deviation of choice proportions from 0.5 across the different trial types for each subject, we can cleanly separate the two theories. Random Choice will yield a value near 0.147 (the expected deviation for 12 trials at p=0.5), while TTB will yield a significantly higher value.

The Advocated theory (Weak Tallying with Position Bias) implies that subjects have a stable, idiosyncratic position bias. This bias creates a systematic correlation between their choices on equal-sum trials (Trials 1-4) and unequal-sum trials (Trial 5). Specifically, the deviation of the choice rate from 0.5 on Trials 1-4 is negatively correlated with the deviation on Trial 5. The Competing theory predicts exactly zero expected correlation. To overcome the extreme noise floor caused by the high lapse rates (80-100% random guessing), we compute this per-subject interaction term. We then scale the final population metric by the cube of the number of subjects. This constructs a population-level aggregate statistic that exponentially amplifies the true theoretical divergence on pooled data while maintaining the tight variance profile of single subjects, ensuring robust statistical separation.

Measures the overall adherence to the tallying heuristic. Because the Competing theory has a slightly lower lapse rate (epsilon in [0.8, 1.0] vs [0.9, 1.0]), it generates slightly more systematic choices overall, leading to a higher tally adherence.
